problem: End-to-end model-free RL for PointGoal navigation (e.g. DD-PPO) needs billions of frames, and hierarchical RL planners predict waypoints in unknown space via black boxes with no reachability guarantee. Model-based Learning over Subgoals Planning (LSP) had only been tested with laser scans in office-like environments.
motivation: A frontier-based POMDP abstraction gives completeness and data efficiency, but it needs a learned estimator of frontier properties that works with visual sensing in large realistic indoor scenes. The paper asks whether learned frontier properties from semantic maps can match end-to-end RL with far less data.
key_idea: Adapt LSP by using a U-Net on the partial occupancy and semantic map, plus a goal map, to predict per-frontier properties (P_S, R_S, R_E) for model-based expected-cost planning over frontier subgoals.
insight: Learned frontier properties beat the optimistic planner: with the oracle mapper LSP-UNet* gets 88.2 SR / 74.7 SPL vs Optimistic* 87.5 / 70.5, and with the estimated map 82.0 vs 75.9 SR. The gap to DD-PPO is mostly due to the non-learned mapper and the local planner, since the oracle mapper closes most of the SR gap. The approach needs about 230k frames vs 2.5B for DD-PPO.
method: Frontier-subgoal POMDP (LSP): high-level actions are frontiers; expected cost Q follows a Bellman equation using D (Dijkstra travel cost), P_S, R_S and R_E, and the agent picks the minimum-cost action.
U-Net property estimator: takes the local occupancy map, semantic map and 2-channel relative-goal map, and outputs a 3-channel map with P_S, R_S and R_E at frontier pixels.

Training data generation: an optimistic planner runs about 5,000 random trials in each of the 61 train scenes; labels come from the ground-truth map, with R_S the path length via unknown space and R_E a TSP tour on the skeleton of unknown free space.
Loss: BCE on P_S plus 0.01 times L1 on R_S (only where P_S=1) and R_E (only where P_S=0), applied on frontier pixels via masks.

Mapping and frontiers: RGB-D and semantic segmentation are projected to a 5cm top-down occupancy and semantic map; frontiers are 8-connected boundary cells with centroids, and unreachable ones are filtered out.
Local navigation: Fast Marching Method path planning with discrete actions (forward 25cm, turn 30°), replanning every step.

setting.backbone: U-Net (trained from scratch, supervised) for frontier property prediction; Dijkstra and Fast Marching Method planners
setting.training_data: About 230k train / 2k val map-frame tuples generated by an optimistic planner in 61 MP3D train scenes (about 5,000 trials each), with labels from the GT map
setting.observation: Egocentric 90° FoV RGB-D plus GT semantic segmentation, 256x256, noise-free pose
setting.privileged: GT semantic segmentation and noise-free pose; the starred variants additionally use an oracle mapper for occupancy maps

numbers.extra: Mapper built from sensor observations; GT semantic segmentation and noise-free pose; 500 step budget; 0.2m success radius
numbers.evidence: Table 1, Comparison of Point Goal Navigation Methods (MP3D Test), row LSP-UNet

numbers.extra: Oracle mapper producing error-free occupancy maps; GT semantic segmentation and noise-free pose

numbers_note: The paper says the 1008 standard Habitat PointGoal test episodes on MP3D were used.
results: LSP-UNet reaches 82.0 SR / 60.5 SPL and, with an oracle mapper, LSP-UNet* reaches 88.2 / 74.7. That beats ANS (59.3 / 49.6) and the Optimistic planner, and is slightly below DD-PPO (89.0 / 80.0), which uses about 2.5B frames vs 230k.
limitations: The non-learned mapper is noisy and hurts performance; the oracle mapper is needed to be near DD-PPO
The local planner fails in narrow passages
Uses GT semantic segmentation and noise-free poses; the frontier abstraction is specific to 2D navigation maps
